sections.title: Pick the story
sections.intro: "Tell me about the project you're proudest of." You have three candidates in your catalog. Choose the way you would in the room.

questions.prompt: Why build a story catalog before the interview at all?
options: So the interviewer sees a list of your projects
So you never have to reuse the same story twice
So you can memorize each answer word for word
So picking a story is lookup, not invention, under load
questions.explanation: Live, you're already reading the interviewer, managing your impression, and structuring the answer. Searching your whole career on the spot uses up working memory you don't have to spare.

questions.prompt: Your options: (A) a platform migration you drove across three teams over two quarters; (B) a clever caching fix last month; (C) a team-offsite you organized. Which criterion do you apply *first*?
options: Relevance — the closest literal match to "proud"
Uniqueness — the story nobody else would tell
Recency — the most recent story carries the most weight
Scope — the biggest box of breadth, time, and impact
questions.explanation: The order is Scope → Relevance → Uniqueness → Recency. "Proudest" isn't about how you feel. It's a request for your high-water mark.

questions.prompt: So you pick A. Why does Scope beat Recency here, even though B happened last month?
options: They're assessing your high-water mark, not your latest work
Recent stories are often viewed as less reliable
Older stories have more measurable results
Recency only matters for junior candidates
questions.explanation: They want the ceiling of what you can do. Recency still counts, so be cautious with stories 3-5 years old and generally avoid ones 6+ years old, but it's last in the order.

questions.prompt: Later: "Tell me about a conflict." Your migration story had a real disagreement in it. Your only other conflict story is a minor code-style spat. What do you do?
options: Tell the offsite story and reframe it as conflict
Reuse the migration, foregrounding the conflict
Tell the code-style spat — you haven't used it yet
Say you don't have a good conflict example
questions.explanation: Uniqueness matters, but not more than scope and relevance. Your weakest conflict story doesn't beat a strong one just because it's new to this interviewer.

questions.prompt: In the migration, a senior engineer made the final architecture calls; you drove the proof-of-concept. How do you describe your role?
options: Name exactly what you drove, and who made the final call
Leave the senior engineer out to keep it simple
Say you led it — the PoC shaped the whole thing
Say "we" throughout so nobody's role is unclear
questions.explanation: Inflating breaks down under follow-up questions, because you won't have the details. An honest description ("I drove the PoC that shaped the approach; they made the service-boundary calls") is credible and still shows your impact.

questions.prompt: Another question asks about leading a team through a reorg. You've never done that. Best move?
options: Adapt a story and fill in the parts you don't have
Tell an unrelated story that shows leadership
Ask to skip the question and move on
Say so, then answer it as a hypothetical from related work
questions.explanation: "I haven't led at that scale yet, but here's how I'd approach it, based on…" is honest and still shows judgment. Made-up details are the fastest way to lose an interviewer's trust.

questions.prompt: A candidate's catalog has five core stories, all technically complex, all from the same project. What's the gap?
options: Too many core stories — three is the maximum
Nothing — one deep project is the ideal catalog
Signal coverage — they likely lack conflict, growth, etc.
Too technical — stories should avoid technical detail
questions.explanation: Core stories are your best material. Additional stories exist to fill the signal areas your core stories don't cover. Check each of the 8 areas and journal against the ones that are thin.

questions.prompt: You have two strong, roughly equal conflict stories. What technique fits?
questions.snippet: "I have two examples — one a technical architecture disagreement, one about resource allocation with my manager. Which is more useful?"
options: Over-preparation — it sounds rehearsed
The Menu Technique — offer a choice, used sparingly
Table of Contents — previewing your story's themes
A stalling tactic — pick one and commit instead
questions.explanation: It shows depth, buys a moment to think, and makes sure you deliver the signal they actually want. Used every time, it becomes a crutch.

questions.prompt: A candidate interviewing with a frontend-heavy panel has two equal-scope stories: one backend, one frontend. Which criterion breaks the tie?
options: Uniqueness — pick whichever is less common
Recency — pick whichever happened later
Scope — they're equal, so it's a coin flip
Relevance — the audience shapes what resonates
questions.explanation: Relevance includes context: the role, the company, and who's interviewing. When everything else is equal, the story that speaks to the listener's world wins.

questions.prompt: "Tell me about a failure." Candidate A picks a vague, low-stakes miss. Candidate B picks a launch that slipped a month with real customer impact. Who chose better?
options: A — low stakes keep the failure safe to discuss
Neither — never tell a real failure story
B — real consequences deliver more real signal
A — vagueness avoids follow-up questions
questions.explanation: Relevance is a spectrum. Real stakes make the recovery and the lesson believable. Pick a failure that shows growth in skill, not a flaw in character.

questions.prompt: A candidate's best story is seven years old. They're mid-level. Risk?
options: It's only a risk for very senior candidates
None — older stories show long experience
Interviewers can't verify older stories
Interviewers wonder what they've done since
questions.explanation: Stories 6+ years old invite "what have you done lately?" Senior candidates have more leeway, and a career break is a clear reason, but the default is recent material.

questions.prompt: Where should each catalog entry's Actions focus?
options: What *you* did — designing, aligning, deciding, shipping
The timeline of the project, phase by phase
What the team accomplished as a whole
The technical architecture, in full detail
questions.explanation: The template captures your actions across every dimension, including non-technical ones like aligning and communicating. Thinking and deciding count as actions too.
